croatia.text: A wine country whose winemaking goes back some 2,500 years to Greek settlers on the Dalmatian islands of Vis, Hvar and Korčula. Most of its wine is white. Graševina is the most planted grape at 27 percent, then Malvazija Istarska and Plavac Mali Crni.

croatia/dalmatinska-zagora.text: A Croatian appellation for still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine. Its grapes include the local reds Plavac Mali Crni, Babić and Crljenak Kaštelanski and the whites Pošip Bijeli and Maraština, alongside Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay.

croatia/dingac.text: A small Croatian red wine area of about 150 acres on the Pelješac sub-region of Middle and South Dalmatia, made only from Plavac Mali Crni. The wines are dark, full and a little bitter, and can be very high in alcohol. It was the first protected Croatian wine region, in 1961.

croatia/hrvatska-istra.text: A Croatian appellation for still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine. Its grape list includes Malvazija Istarska, Teran, Muscat Blanc and Žlahtina, plus Merlot, Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon. Its communes include Buje, Buzet, Barban and Kanfanar.

croatia/hrvatsko-podunavlje.text: A Croatian appellation for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine, spread over some 60 communes including Beli Manastir, Darda and Donji Miholjac. Allowed grapes include Furmint, Riesling, Kadarka, Blaufrankisch, Gewürztraminer and Pinot Noir.

croatia/hrvatsko-primorje.text: A Croatian appellation for still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine, with communes such as Krk, Cres, Opatija and Novi Vinodolski. Its grapes include Malvazija Istarska, Žlahtina, Teran, Babić and Plavac Mali Crni, as well as Chardonnay and Merlot.

croatia/istocna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.text: A large Croatian appellation of 133 communes, including Beli Manastir, Belišće and Bizovac, for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Allowed grapes include Furmint, Riesling, Kadarka, Blaufrankisch, Gewürztraminer and Pinot Noir.

croatia/moslavina.text: A Croatian appellation of 15 communes, including Kutina, Garešnica, Ivanić-Grad and Čazma, for wine, semi-sparkling wine and sparkling wine. Grapes on its list include Škrlet Bijeli, Kraljevina Crvena and Dišeća Ranina Bijela, alongside Furmint and Riesling.

croatia/muskat-momjanski.text: A Croatian appellation for wine from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, its only listed grape. It covers a single commune, Buje.

croatia/plesivica.text: A Croatian appellation of 11 communes, including Jastrebarsko, Samobor, Ozalj and Žumberak. It allows wine, semi-sparkling wine and sparkling wine from grapes such as Kraljevina Crvena, Lipovina, Furmint, Riesling and Pinot Noir.

croatia/pokuplje.text: A Croatian appellation of 36 communes, including Glina, Duga Resa and Jasenovac, for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Its grapes include Škrlet Bijeli, Štajerska Belina, Šipelj and Zelenac Slatki, plus Furmint, Riesling and Pinot Noir.

croatia/ponikve.text: A Croatian appellation in the commune of Ston, for wine and wine from raisined grapes. It allows only three grapes: the white Maraština and Pošip Bijeli and the red Plavac Mali Crni.

croatia/prigorje-bilogora.text: A Croatian appellation of 48 communes, including Bjelovar, Dugo Selo and Grubišno Polje, for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Its grapes include Škrlet Bijeli, Kleščec Bijeli, Kraljevina Crvena and Štajerska Belina, plus Furmint and Riesling.

croatia/primorska-hrvatska.text: One of the largest Croatian appellations, with 180 communes and a list of over 90 grapes. It allows still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine, from whites such as Malvazija Istarska, Žlahtina, Pošip Bijeli and Grk to reds such as Plavac Mali Crni, Babić and Teran.

croatia/sjeverna-dalmacija.text: A Croatian appellation in northern Dalmatia, with communes such as Biograd Na Moru, Nin, Primošten and Pašman. It allows still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine from grapes including Babić, Plavac Mali Crni, Maraština, Pošip Bijeli and Debit.

croatia/slavonija.text: A Croatian appellation of 73 communes, including Daruvar, for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Allowed grapes include Furmint, Riesling, Kadarka, Blaufrankisch, Gewürztraminer and Pinot Noir.

croatia/srednja-i-juzna-dalmacija.text: A Croatian appellation in middle and southern Dalmatia, with communes such as Hvar, Korčula, Dubrovnik and Konavle. Its grapes include Plavac Mali Crni, Babić, Crljenak Kaštelanski, Pošip Bijeli, Maraština and Grk. It allows still, sparkling, semi-sparkling and liqueur wine.

croatia/zagorje-meimurje.text: A Croatian appellation of 94 communes for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Its grapes include Kraljevina Crvena, Lipovina and Kavčina Crna, plus Furmint, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Gewürztraminer.

croatia/zapadna-kontinentalna-hrvatska.text: A large Croatian appellation of 203 communes, including Bjelovar, Berek and Brdovec, for still, semi-sparkling and sparkling wine. Its grapes include Škrlet Bijeli, Kraljevina Crvena, Furmint, Riesling and Pinot Noir.

slovenia.text: A wine country with about 55,000 acres of vineyards, where about 75 percent of production is white. Welschriesling, Refosco and Chardonnay are the most planted grapes. Its three principal regions are Drava, Lower Sava and the Littoral.

slovenia/bela-krajina.text: A Slovenian appellation in the communes of Metlika, Semič and Črnomelj, for wine and sparkling wine. The area grows above all Blaufränkisch (19 percent) and Welschriesling (17), with Kraljevina and Žametovka also planted.

slovenia/belokranjec.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine made from grapes such as Kraljevina, Laški Rizling, Renski Rizling, Chardonnay and Sauvignon. It covers the communes of Metlika, Semič and Črnomelj.

slovenia/bizeljcan.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine, in communes such as Brežice, Krško, Sevnica and Kozje. Allowed grapes include Laški Rizling, Modra Frankinja, Žametovka and Zweigelt.

slovenia/bizeljsko-sremic.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine, in communes such as Brežice, Krško, Sevnica and Kozje. It grows above all Blaufränkisch and Welschriesling (19 percent each), then Žametovka at 15.

slovenia/cvicek.text: A Slovenian wine from Lower Carniola, unusual for blending white and red grapes. It is low in alcohol, at 8.5 to 10 percent. Long known as a sour, poor wine, it has become popular with locals and visitors.

slovenia/dolenjska.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine, in communes such as Krško, Brežice and Litija. Žametovka is the most planted grape at 39 percent, followed by Blaufränkisch at 19 and Welschriesling at 10.

slovenia/goriska-brda.text: A hilly area in western Slovenia, on the right bank of the Soča (Isonzo) River and shared with Italy, mostly making white wine. Ribolla Gialla is the most planted grape at 21 percent, then Chardonnay and Merlot at 16 each.

slovenia/kras.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine, in the communes of Komen, Miren-Kostanjevica and Sežana. Refosco makes up 73 percent of plantings, followed by Malvazija Istarska at 9 and Vitovska Grganja at 6.

slovenia/metliska-crnina.text: A Slovenian appellation with a short grape list: Žametovka, Modra Frankinja, Gamay, Modri Pinot, Portugalka, Zweigelt and Šentlovrenka. It covers the communes of Metlika, Semič and Črnomelj.

slovenia/pgis.text: A group of Slovenian protected geographical indications. It holds three areas: Posavje, Primorska and Podravje.

slovenia/prekmurje.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine. Welschriesling makes up 32 percent of plantings, then Chardonnay at 11 and Riesling at 10, with some Furmint and Sauvignon Blanc.

slovenia/slovenska-istra.text: Slovene Istria, the northern part of the Istrian peninsula, in southwest Slovenia, with towns such as Koper, Izola and Piran. Refosco makes up 41 percent of plantings and Malvazija Istarska 34 percent. It allows wine and sparkling wine.

slovenia/stajerska-slovenija.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine. Welschriesling is the most planted at 19 percent, then Sauvignon Blanc at 12 and Chardonnay at 9, with Riesling and Furmint also grown.

slovenia/teran.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine made only from Refošk, in communes such as Sežana, Komen and Nova Gorica.

slovenia/vipavska-dolina.text: A Slovenian appellation for wine and sparkling wine, in communes such as Ajdovščina and Nova Gorica. Merlot is the most planted grape at 14 percent, then Malvazija Istarska at 12, with Sauvignon Blanc and Ribolla Gialla at 10 each.

portugal/algarve.text: A Portuguese PGI where Negramoll and Castelão are the most planted grapes, at 18 and 17 percent. Touriga Nacional, Síria and Tempranillo follow at 7 percent each.

portugal/beira-interior.text: A Portuguese DOC in central Portugal, created in 2005 by joining three smaller regions. It allows wine and sparkling wine from grapes such as Alfrocheiro, Baga, Marufo, Arinto, Fonte Cal and Malvasia Fina.

portugal/biscoitos.text: A wine region on Terceira island in the Azores, known mainly for fortified wines. Its rules allow only liqueur wine, from grapes including Verdelho, Arinto, Terrantez, Sercial and Malvasia.

portugal/graciosa.text: A wine region on the island of Graciosa in the Azores, known for light-bodied table wines. Its grapes include Verdelho, Arinto, Boal Branco, Malvasia and Sercial.

portugal/lafoes.text: A Portuguese wine region near Viseu that overlaps the Dão and Vinho Verde DOCs, known for acidic, light-bodied red and white wines. Allowed grapes include Arinto, Cercial and Rabo de Ovelha, and Touriga Nacional, Jaen and Amaral.

portugal/lagoa.text: A DOC in the Algarve centered on the Lagoa municipality, historically known for fortified wine and now making more table wine. Allowed grapes include Touriga Nacional, Castelão, Negra Mole, Syrah, Arinto and Síria.

portugal/lagos.text: A Portuguese appellation for wine, covering communes such as Aljezur and Budens. Allowed grapes include Touriga Nacional, Castelão, Negra Mole, Aragonez, Arinto and Síria.

portugal/madeirense.text: A Portuguese appellation for wine. Its grape list is broad, with Verdelho, Sercial, Tinta Negra, Bastardo and several Malvasias, alongside Touriga Nacional, Syrah and Chardonnay.

portugal/pico.text: A wine region on the island of Pico in the Azores, known mainly for fortified wines and for its UNESCO listed vineyard landscape. Its rules allow only liqueur wine, from grapes such as Verdelho, Arinto, Sercial and Terrantez do Pico.

portugal/portimao.text: A DOC in the Algarve centered on the Portimão municipality, between Lagos to the west and Lagoa to the east. Allowed grapes include Touriga Nacional, Castelão, Trincadeira, Negra Mole, Arinto and Síria.

portugal/tavira.text: A DOC in the Algarve centered on the Tavira municipality and reaching the Spanish border. Allowed grapes include Touriga Nacional, Castelão, Negra Mole, Arinto, Síria, Tamarez and Diagalves.

portugal/tavora-varosa.text: A Portuguese DOC in the Beiras for still and sparkling wine. The wines of its former Encostas da Nave area are very like those of the Douro.

portugal/terras-da-beira.text: A Portuguese PGI where Rufete and Síria lead plantings at 16 percent each, followed by Tempranillo at 15 and Marufo at 10.

portugal/terras-de-cister.text: A Portuguese PGI where Malvasia Fina is the most planted grape at 19 percent, followed by Touriga Franca at 13, Trincadeira at 8 and Palomino Fino at 7.

portugal/terras-madeirenses.text: A Portuguese regional wine area on Madeira and Porto Santo, for simpler non-fortified wines. The better known fortified wines of Madeira are sold under the separate Madeira DOC.

portugal/tras-os-montes.text: A DOC in the northeastern corner of Portugal, with vineyards across a wide range of altitudes. Cooler high sites give light-bodied wines and lower sites give full-bodied, highly alcoholic ones. Tempranillo, Trincadeira and Trousseau are widely planted.

armenia.text: Armenian wine comes from one of the world's oldest wine regions, with clear evidence of production from the 5th millennium BCE. Kangun and Rkatsiteli are the most planted grapes at 40 and 29 percent, then Areni Sev. Quality has changed since the end of the Soviet era.

armenia/armavir.text: An Armenian wine area where Kangun makes up 40 percent of plantings and Rkatsiteli 37 percent, followed by Megrabuir at 9.
